opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, so the core issue is that if you want to train a frontier model in a single location, you increasingly need a huge amount of power concentrated at one site. We're talking about training runs that, if current scaling trends continue, could require multiple gigawatts by the end of the decade. Finding a single site with that much spare grid capacity, or building the generation and transmission to support it, is really hard. Interconnection queues are long, permitting takes years, and utilities are often not set up to deliver that kind of load to one spot on short notice.

Geographically distributed training relaxes that constraint. Instead of needing, say, five gigawatts in one place, you could tap a gigawatt here, a gigawatt there, across several sites, maybe in different states or regions where there's existing slack in the grid or cheap generation available. That's a much easier problem to solve, because there are many more locations with a few hundred megawatts to a gigawatt of available capacity than there are locations with several gigawatts.

The obvious objection is communication. Training involves synchronizing gradients across all the chips, and the bandwidth between data centers is far lower than the bandwidth within a cluster. But when we looked at this carefully, the picture is more optimistic than people often assume. Long-haul fiber bandwidth is substantial and can be expanded relatively cheaply compared to the cost of the compute itself. And there are algorithmic approaches, things like doing more local steps between synchronizations, compressing gradients, or overlapping communication with computation, that reduce how much data you need to move and how often. Methods in the spirit of DiLoCo show you can sync much less frequently without losing much performance.

So our rough view was that distributed training across multiple data centers is quite feasible for very large runs, maybe with some modest efficiency penalty. That means power is less likely to be a hard binding constraint on scaling than it would be if everything had to happen at one site. It doesn't make the power problem go away, since total energy demand is still enormous, but it turns it from a question of whether you can get a massive amount of power in a single place to whether you can get it in aggregate across the country, which is a much more tractable problem.

r001.rationale: The response says frontier training requires enormous power concentrated at a single site and that finding or supplying that much power in one place is difficult.

r002.rationale: It explains that training across several locations can draw on existing grid capacity or cheap generation at each site, making large runs more feasible.

r003.rationale: It does not mention using roughly 0.5% of US installed power capacity or argue that this use is justified by AI’s industrial importance.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the basic observation is that the power constraints people worry about are really constraints on concentrating power in a single location. If you want to build a single training cluster that draws, say, five or ten gigawatts, you run into very real bottlenecks: you need to site it near enough generation, you need transmission capacity, you need the grid interconnection approvals, and those things take years. The US grid as a whole has something like a terawatt of capacity, so at the level of the whole system, a few tens of gigawatts for AI isn't actually that large. The problem is that it's very hard to pull a large fraction of that into one place.

So distributed training is a way of relaxing that constraint. Instead of one site that needs five gigawatts, you have five or ten sites that each need a few hundred megawatts to a gigawatt, and those are much easier to find. There's existing data center capacity, there are places with stranded or cheap power, there are utilities that can accommodate a few hundred megawatts without building new generation. You're essentially spreading the load across the grid rather than demanding that it be concentrated.

The question is what you give up when you do this. The main cost is bandwidth and latency between sites. Within a single data center, you have very high-bandwidth interconnect, and standard parallelism strategies rely on that. Between data centers you have maybe orders of magnitude less bandwidth and much higher latency. But I think there are a couple of reasons to be fairly optimistic here. One is that if you look at the actual communication requirements of large training runs, data parallelism across sites is pretty feasible. You can do a fairly large chunk of compute locally, exchange gradients or model updates between sites at relatively infrequent intervals, and the bandwidth you need for that is within what you can get from existing or buildable fiber links. The sort of analyses we've done suggest that, with the right approach to partitioning the training run, you could coordinate on the order of tens of gigawatts across multiple sites without a very large efficiency penalty.

The second reason is that there's a lot of algorithmic headroom. Things like reducing how often you synchronize, compressing the communications, or using asynchronous updates all trade a small amount of training efficiency for a big reduction in bandwidth requirements. And the incentives to figure this out are strong: if the alternative is that you simply can't build the cluster, then a few percent loss in efficiency is a very good trade.

So my overall view is that power is a real constraint, but it's more of a constraint on the timing and geography of buildout than a hard ceiling on how much compute you can bring to bear on a single training run. Distributed training essentially lets you draw on the aggregate capacity of the grid rather than the local capacity at one site, and I think that pushes the point at which power becomes binding out by a fair amount, maybe several years.

r001.rationale: It says the bottleneck comes from trying to concentrate several gigawatts at one site, where generation, transmission, and grid approvals are difficult.

r002.rationale: It explains that multiple sites can draw on existing data centers, stranded or cheap power, and grid capacity across locations to support much larger training runs.

r003.rationale: It discusses tens of gigawatts and tradeoffs that could make distributed training worthwhile, but does not say that using roughly 0.5% of US installed capacity for a 2030-scale run is justified by AI’s industrial importance.

astra-6.text:
The basic idea is that you don’t have to get all the power for a training run in one place. If you need a gigawatt of power at a single site, you need a very large grid connection, and getting that built can take a long time. But if you can spread training across several sites, you can draw on power that’s available in different locations.

The challenge is communication. During training, the chips need to exchange a lot of information, and doing that across long distances introduces latency and bandwidth constraints. So the question is whether you can organize training so that most communication happens locally, with less frequent communication between sites, without losing too much efficiency.

If that works well, it gives you much more flexibility in where you build. You could use several smaller power connections instead of waiting for one enormous connection. It wouldn’t eliminate the total energy requirement, but it could ease the bottleneck of getting enough power delivered to a particular location.

r002.rationale: It explains that training across several sites can draw on power available in different locations and use multiple smaller power connections, enabling more flexibility in scaling.

r003.rationale: It does not mention 0.5% of US installed power capacity, a 2030-scale run, or judging that such usage is justified by AI's industrial importance.

sol-6.1.text:
One way to ease the power bottleneck is to avoid requiring all of the power to be available in a single location. If you want to build a very large training cluster, you need an enormous amount of electricity at one site, and getting that connection can take a long time. There might be plenty of power available elsewhere, but you can’t use it if all of your chips have to sit in the same data center.

Geographically distributed training could let you spread that workload across several sites, tapping into power wherever it’s available. That gives you more flexibility in where you build, and potentially lets you use existing power infrastructure instead of waiting for a huge new connection.

The challenge is communication. During training, the chips need to exchange information, and communication between distant data centers is slower and more constrained than communication within a single facility. So you need methods that do more computation locally and communicate less frequently, without losing too much training efficiency. If those methods work well enough, you could relax the requirement to concentrate so much power in one place. It wouldn’t eliminate the total energy requirement, but it could make that energy much easier to supply.

r001.rationale: It explains that a very large training cluster needs enormous power at one site and that concentrating chips in one data center limits access to power elsewhere.

r002.rationale: It says distributed training can spread the workload across several sites, use power available in different locations, and tap existing power infrastructure.

r003.rationale: It does not discuss using roughly 0.5% of US installed power capacity or whether that use is justified by AI’s industrial importance.
